summary: This RFC defines one-way packet loss metrics that describe loss episodes, meaning maximal runs of consecutively lost probe packets. Applications are sensitive not only to average loss rate but to how the losses are distributed, which the earlier loss metric did not capture.

eli5.summary: Losing ten packets one at a time is different from losing ten in a row. This defines ways to measure runs of lost packets, not just the total.

questions: how to measure bursty packet loss
what is a packet loss episode
how does geometric probing measure packet loss
what is a loss pair in ippm
subtitle: Metrics that measure how packet losses cluster into episodes, not just the average loss rate.

tldr.problem: The existing one-way loss metric gives only an average loss ratio, but applications are sensitive to how losses are distributed over time, in episodes of consecutive lost packets.
tldr.mechanism: Probe packets are sent in pairs at a fixed separation, launched at random geometric intervals. The counts of the four possible outcomes for each pair yield loss ratio, average loss episode duration and loss episode frequency.
tldr.outcome: A pair of metrics (episode frequency and average duration) generalizes the single loss ratio without assuming any loss model, and the ratio can be recovered from them.

today: RFC 6534 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It generalizes the single loss ratio of RFC 2680.

sections.title: Why Average Loss Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The IETF already has a one-way packet loss metric (RFC 2680) that reports a single average loss ratio over a probe stream. Packet loss is bursty, though, so a single ratio does not say how a stream is affected. RFC 6534 defines loss episode metrics, where a loss episode is a maximal set of consecutively lost packets.

The RFC gives an example: MPEG video may be sensitive to loss of the I-frame in a group of pictures, but more losses within a short episode do no further harm, since the damage is already done.

The metrics are derived metrics under the IPPM framework (RFC 2330), built on the singleton loss metric of RFC 2680.
sections.eli5: It matters whether you drop one marble now and then or a whole handful at once. The average hides the difference, so this RFC measures the streaks.

sections.title: Empirical Metrics Instead of Loss Models
sections.content:
The simplest model, independent Bernoulli loss, does not describe real loss. Markov models such as Gilbert and Elliott have a good state and a bad state, but larger state spaces get cumbersome to estimate and predict. Related standards work includes loss pattern sample metrics (RFC 3357) and VoIP burst metrics (RFC 3611).

The RFC therefore picks metrics that are empirical and model independent. They have three stated properties: they need no model such as Markovian loss, their units compare directly with application tolerance for frequency and duration of episodes, and they are the smallest step beyond a single ratio, namely two metrics. The usual ratio is recovered by dividing average episode duration by episode frequency.
sections.eli5: Instead of guessing a complicated theory about how losses happen, the RFC just counts what you actually see.

sections.title: Loss Pairs
sections.content:
The basic measurement is a Loss Pair (l1, l2) for two packets sent from Src to Dst at times T1 and T2, with T2 greater than T1. Each value is 0 for a packet received and 1 for a packet lost. There are four outcomes: (1,1) both lost, (1,0) only the first lost, (0,1) only the second lost and (0,0) both received.

The singleton metric is named Type-P-One-way-Bi-Packet-Loss. Its parameters are Src, Dst, T1, T2, a selection function F that says which two packets of a stream are used, and the packet type P. Methodology and error sources are taken from RFC 2680 and apply to both packets.

A Type-P-One-way-Bi-Packet-Loss-Stream is a set of n Loss Pairs. Pairs may be sampled from an existing stream and need not be consecutive in it.
sections.eli5: Send two letters one after the other. Each one either arrives or gets lost, so there are four possible results.

sections.title: Geometric Probing
sections.content:
The active methodology is Type-P-One-way-Bi-Packet-Loss-Geometric-Stream. Evenly spaced times Ti = T0 + i*d are launch opportunities, where T0 is a randomly selected start time and d is the spacing. At each, a pair is launched with probability q, using the packets at Ti and T(i+1). The spacing between launch times equals the spacing inside a pair, so a pair launched at Ti and another at T(i+1) share a packet. The count m of pairs can be below n because not every instant launches.

Gaps between pairs follow a geometric distribution, so this generalizes Poisson probing. It differs from back-to-back packet pairs used to probe bandwidth. The separation within a pair is the time resolution at which episodes are told apart. The method estimates average episode length without measuring full episodes, because that information is encoded in the relative frequencies of the four outcomes. Choosing the spacing is out of scope. A key error source is the sending host: too little CPU may make it miss its schedule, which gets harder with a spacing of 100 microseconds than 100 milliseconds.
sections.eli5: At regular ticks you flip a weighted coin to decide whether to send a pair of test packets. Counting how the pairs turn out reveals how long loss streaks are.

sections.title: From Pair Counts to Episode Numbers
sections.content:
Four intermediate proto-metrics are computed from Loss-Pair-Counts, the numbers N(i,j) of pairs with each outcome. They are not expected to be reported on their own. They are in packet counts, independent of the real time between probes.

  • Bi-Packet-Loss-Ratio is (N(1,0) + N(1,1))/n, equivalent to the average loss metric of RFC 2680.
  • Duration Number is (2*N(1,1) + N(0,1) + N(1,0)) / (N(0,1) + N(1,0)) if N(0,1) + N(1,0) > 0. It is 0 if no probes were lost and undefined if all were lost.
  • Frequency Number is the Ratio divided by the Duration Number. It is 0 if no probes were lost and 1 if all were lost.

The RFC points to a published analysis showing that for an ideal sample with q = 1 the Duration Number is exactly the average number of packets in a loss episode. For q below 1 the metrics are estimators of that ideal.
sections.eli5: You tally up the four kinds of results. A little arithmetic on the tallies tells you how long the streaks are and how often they start.

sections.title: The Three Reported Metrics
sections.content:
Three final metrics share the geometric stream parameters Src, Dst, T0, d, n, q, F and P.

  • Geometric-Stream-Ratio: the Bi-Packet-Loss-Ratio, a decimal number in the interval [0,1], estimating the fraction of packets lost.
  • Geometric-Stream-Episode-Duration: the Duration Number multiplied by d, a non-negative number of seconds, estimating the average loss episode length. Dividing by d gives the length in packets.
  • Geometric-Stream-Episode-Frequency: the Frequency Number divided by d, a positive number, estimating how often episodes start (or finish) per unit time.

Each refers back to the methodology and error discussion of the probing section, and notes that for q below 1 the results are statistical estimators of the ideal case.
sections.eli5: You end up with three numbers: how much is lost, how long a loss streak lasts, and how often streaks begin.

sections.title: Relation to the Gilbert Model
sections.content:
The Gilbert-Elliott model is a two-state Markov chain with Good and Bad states. In the simplest case the Good loss ratio is 0 and the Bad is 1, leaving two parameters, P(g|b) and P(b|g).

Taking the ratio as r and the average episode duration as m, the RFC equates r = P(b|g)/(P(b|g) + P(g|b)) and m/d = 1/P(g|b). Inverting gives P(g|b) = d/m and P(b|g) = d/m/(1/r - 1). So the model-free metrics can be turned into Gilbert parameters when that model is wanted.
sections.eli5: If you do want a simple good-day, bad-day theory of losses, you can work its numbers out from these measurements.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC does not specify an implementation, so it does not directly affect Internet security. It names two concerns. Active probes inject packets, so parameters MUST be chosen so they add trivial traffic, or results are skewed and in extreme cases congestion and denial of service can follow.

The measurements can also be harmed: routers might treat probe traffic differently, and an attacker injecting artificial traffic accepted as legitimate would lower the measured loss rate. Methodologies SHOULD reduce the chance probes can be told from normal traffic, and digital signatures may guard against injection. Privacy concerns are limited because no user data is released.
sections.eli5: Test packets must not clog the road they measure, and nobody should be able to fake test packets to make the road look better.

data.title: Bi-Packet-Loss-Episode-Duration-Number
data.code:
(2*N(1,1) + N(0,1) + N(1,0)) / (N(0,1) + N(1,0))   if N(0,1) + N(1,0) > 0
0           if N(0,1) + N(1,0) + N(1,1) = 0  (no probe packets lost)
Undefined   if N(0,1) + N(1,0) + N(0,0) = 0  (all probe packets lost)
